metadata.title: Sampling Signals with Finite Rate of Innovation
metadata.venue: IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, Vol. 50, No. 6
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Rate of Innovation
nodes.statement: For a signal $x(t)$ with parametric representation $x(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{r=0}^{R-1} c_{r,k} \varphi_r(t - t_k)$, define a counting function $C_x(t_a, t_b)$ that counts the number of degrees of freedom in $x(t)$ over $[t_a, t_b]$. The rate of innovation is $\rho = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{\tau} C_x(-\tau/2, \tau/2)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The rate of innovation of a signal is the average number of real-valued degrees of freedom per unit of time.

nodes.name: Signal with Finite Rate of Innovation
nodes.statement: A signal with a finite rate of innovation is a signal whose parametric representation is given by $x(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{r=0}^{R-1} c_{r,k} \varphi_r(t - t_k)$ and with a finite $\rho$ as defined in (7).
nodes.statement_clean: A signal is FRI if its parametric form has only finitely many degrees of freedom per unit time.

nodes.name: Local Rate of Innovation
nodes.statement: Given a window of size $\tau$, the local rate of innovation at time $t$ is $\rho_\tau(t) = \frac{1}{\tau} C_x(t - \tau/2, t + \tau/2)$. The maximal local rate is $\rho_{\max}(\tau) = \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \rho_\tau(t)$, and as $\tau \to \infty$, $\rho_\tau(t) \to \rho$.
nodes.statement_clean: The local rate of innovation measures degrees of freedom inside a sliding window.

nodes.name: Annihilating Filter
nodes.statement: A filter $A(z)$ is called an annihilating filter of a signal $X[m]$ when $(A * X)[m] = \sum_l A[l] X[m-l] = 0$ for all $m$.
nodes.statement_clean: An annihilating filter is a discrete filter whose convolution with the target signal is identically zero.

nodes.name: B-Spline of Degree d
nodes.statement: The B-spline of degree $d$ is $\beta^d(t) = \beta^0(t) * \beta^0(t) * \cdots * \beta^0(t)$ ($d+1$ convolutions), where the box spline $\beta^0(t) = 1$ for $t \in [0,1]$ and $0$ elsewhere. The support of $\beta^d(t/T)$ has length $(d+1)T$.
nodes.statement_clean: B-splines are repeated convolutions of the box (rectangular) function.
nodes.origin_citation: Unser, Splines: A perfect fit for signal and image processing, 1999

nodes.name: Bilevel Signal
nodes.statement: A bilevel signal $x(t)$ is an infinite-length continuous-time signal that takes only two values $0$ and $1$, completely represented by an initial condition $x(t_0)$ and the sequence of transition values $\{t_k\}$ at which it switches between $0$ and $1$.
nodes.statement_clean: A bilevel signal is a 0/1-valued signal characterized by its transition times.

nodes.name: Sampling with Smoothing Kernel
nodes.statement: Filtered version $\tilde{x}(t) = \langle h(\tau - t), x(\tau) \rangle$, sampled uniformly with period $T$ to give $y_n = \tilde{x}(nT) = \langle h(\tau - nT), x(\tau) \rangle$.

nodes.name: Whittaker-Shannon Reconstruction
nodes.statement: If $x(t)$ is bandlimited with bandwidth $\omega_0$, then $x(t) = \sum_n y_n \operatorname{sinc}(t/T - n)$ with $T = \pi/\omega_0$, where $\operatorname{sinc}(t) = \sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)$.

nodes.name: Poisson Summation Identity for Periodic Diracs
nodes.statement: A periodic stream of Diracs $x(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c_k \delta(t - t_k - n\tau)$ has Fourier series coefficients $X[m] = \frac{1}{\tau} \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k e^{-j 2\pi m t_k / \tau}$.

nodes.name: Annihilating Filter for Sum of Exponentials
nodes.statement: The signal $X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k u_k^m$, where $c_k, u_k \in \mathbb{C}$, is annihilated by the filter $A(z) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} (1 - u_k z^{-1})$.
nodes.statement_clean: A finite linear combination of complex exponentials is annihilated by the polynomial whose roots are those exponential bases.

nodes.name: Annihilating Filter with Multiple Roots
nodes.statement: The signal $X[m] = m^r u_0^m$ is annihilated by the filter $A(z) = (1 - u_0 z^{-1})^{r+1}$ with $r+1$ poles at $u_0$. More generally, $X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} P_{r_k}(m) u_k^m$ (with $P_{r_k}$ a polynomial of degree at most $r_k$) is annihilated by $A(z) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} (1 - u_k z^{-1})^{r_k+1}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Polynomial-weighted exponentials are annihilated by filters with repeated roots.

nodes.name: Bilevel Signal Recovery from Box-Spline Samples
nodes.statement: A bilevel signal $x(t)$ with initial condition $x(t_0) = 0$ is uniquely determined from the samples $y_n = \langle \beta^0(t/T - n), x(t) \rangle$ if and only if there is at most one transition $t_k$ in each interval $[nT, (n+1)T)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A bilevel signal is reconstructible from box-spline samples iff each sampling interval contains at most one transition.
assumptions: sampling kernel is the box spline $\beta^0$
conclusions: unique recovery $\iff$ at most one transition per interval $[nT, (n+1)T)$

nodes.name: Bilevel Signal Recovery from Hat-Spline Samples
nodes.statement: An infinite-length bilevel signal $x(t)$ with initial condition $x(t_0) = 0$ is uniquely determined from the samples $y_n = \langle \beta^1(t/T - n), x(t) \rangle$ (hat sampling kernel) if and only if there are at most two transitions $t_k$ in each interval $[nT, (n+2)T)$.
nodes.statement_clean: With a hat (degree-1) spline kernel, a bilevel signal is reconstructible iff every length-$2T$ window has at most two transitions.
assumptions: sampling kernel is the hat spline $\beta^1$
conclusions: unique recovery $\iff$ at most two transitions per interval $[nT, (n+2)T)$

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem for Periodic Stream of Diracs
nodes.statement: Let $x(t)$ be a periodic stream of $K$ Diracs of period $\tau$, weights $c_k$ at locations $t_k \in [0,\tau)$. With sampling kernel $h(t) = B \operatorname{sinc}(Bt)$ where $B \geq \rho = 2K/\tau$, sampled at $N \geq 2M+1$ uniform locations $t_n = nT$ ($T = \tau/N$), the samples $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$ are a sufficient characterization of $x(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A periodic stream of K Diracs can be exactly recovered from at least 2K+1 sinc-filtered uniform samples per period.

nodes.name: Spectral Extrapolation via Annihilating Filter Recursion
nodes.statement: Given the annihilating filter $A(z) = \sum_{l=0}^{K} A[l] z^{-l}$ with $A[0]=1$ and the spectrum $X[m]$ for $m = 0, \ldots, K-1$, the entire spectrum is recovered by $X[m] = -\sum_{l=1}^{K} A[l] X[m-l]$. For $m < 0$, use $X[-m] = \overline{X[m]}$ since $x(t)$ is real.
nodes.statement_clean: Once the annihilating filter is known, the rest of the spectrum follows by a linear recursion.
conclusions: full spectrum recovered via $X[m] = -\sum_{l=1}^{K} A[l] X[m-l]$
nodes.notes: Numerically marginal because A(z) has zeros on the unit circle, so the recursion is only marginally stable in practice.

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem for Periodic Nonuniform Splines
nodes.statement: Let $x(t)$ be a periodic nonuniform spline with period $\tau$, containing $K$ pieces of maximum degree $R$ (its $(R+1)$-th derivative is a periodic stream of $K$ weighted Diracs). With sinc kernel $h(t) = B \operatorname{sinc}(Bt)$, $B \geq \rho = 2K/\tau$, and $N \geq 2K+1$ uniform samples at $t_n = nT$, $T = \tau/N$, $x(t)$ is uniquely represented by $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$.
nodes.statement_clean: Periodic nonuniform splines with K knots can be sampled at the rate 2K and recovered exactly.
assumptions: $x(t)$ is a $\tau$-periodic nonuniform spline with $K$ knots, max degree $R$

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem for Periodic Stream of Differentiated Diracs
nodes.statement: Let $x(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \sum_{r=0}^{R_k - 1} c_{r,k} \delta^{(r)}(t - t_k - n\tau)$ be a periodic stream of differentiated Diracs of period $\tau$. With kernel $h(t) = B \operatorname{sinc}(Bt)$, $B \geq \rho = (K + \sum_k R_k)/\tau$, and uniform samples $t_n = nT$, the samples $y_n$ characterize $x(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Streams of differentiated Diracs admit the same sinc-sampling guarantee with rate equal to total degrees of freedom.
assumptions: $x(t)$ stream of differentiated Diracs with $K$ locations and orders $R_k$

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem for Periodic Piecewise Polynomials
nodes.statement: Let $x(t)$ be a periodic piecewise polynomial with period $\tau$, $K$ pieces of maximum degree $R$ (its $(R+1)$-th derivative is a stream of differentiated Diracs). With sinc kernel $h(t) = B \operatorname{sinc}(Bt)$, $B \geq \rho = K(R+1)/\tau$, and $N$ uniform samples at $t_n = nT$, $T = \tau/N$, $x(t)$ is uniquely represented by $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$.
nodes.statement_clean: Periodic piecewise polynomials are sampled exactly at their innovation rate K(R+1)/tau.
assumptions: $x(t)$ is a $\tau$-periodic piecewise polynomial with $K$ pieces, max degree $R$

nodes.name: Conditions C1 and C2 (Sinc Kernel for Finite Diracs)
nodes.statement: C1: $\operatorname{Rank}(S) = K$ where $S$ is the $(N-K) \times K$ matrix in the annihilating equation for the finite-Diracs/sinc system. C2: $\operatorname{Rank}(H) = K$ where $H$ is the matrix used to solve for the Dirac weights once locations are known.

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem with Sinc Kernel (Finite Diracs)
nodes.statement: Given a finite stream of $K$ weighted Diracs $x(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k \delta(t - t_k)$ and a sinc sampling kernel $h(t) = B \operatorname{sinc}(Bt)$ with $BT = 1$, if conditions C1 and C2 are satisfied, then the $N \geq 2K+1$ samples $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$ are a sufficient representation of the signal.
nodes.statement_clean: Finite Diracs can be reconstructed from 2K+1 sinc-filtered samples under two rank conditions.

nodes.name: Sampling Theorem with Gaussian Kernel (Finite Diracs)
nodes.statement: Given a finite stream of $K$ weighted Diracs and a Gaussian sampling kernel $h(t) = e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, if $N \geq 2K$, then the samples $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$ are sufficient to reconstruct the signal. After extracting roots $u_k$ via the annihilating filter, locations are $t_k = \sigma^2 T^{-1} \ln(u_k)$ and weights $c_k = a_k e^{-t_k^2/(2\sigma^2)}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Finite Diracs can be reconstructed from 2K Gaussian-filtered samples by reducing to the exponential annihilating-filter setup.
conclusions: $N$ samples suffice for reconstruction with $t_k$, $c_k$ recovered as stated

nodes.name: B-Spline Local Sampling Conjecture
nodes.statement: Using a B-spline kernel of degree $d$, a local rate of innovation $\rho_{\max}((d+1)T) \leq (d+1)/((d+1)T)$ ensures uniqueness of the local reconstruction of bilevel signals.
nodes.statement_clean: Splines of degree d should give unique local reconstruction whenever the local innovation rate is bounded appropriately.

nodes.name: Annihilating Filter Method
nodes.statement: Three-stage procedure that recovers the locations $u_k$ and weights $c_k$ in $X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k u_k^m$ via a Yule-Walker solve, root finding of $A(z)$, and a Vandermonde solve.
nodes.statement_clean: The core algorithm of the paper: extract spectral parameters via three structured linear solves.
nodes.pseudocode: Step 1: Solve the Toeplitz/Yule-Walker system $\sum_{l=0}^{K} A[l] X[m-l] = 0$ with $A[0]=1$ for the filter coefficients $\{A[l]\}$ (use SVD; in noisy case, take the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue of $X^H X$). Step 2: Find the locations $u_k$ as roots of $A(z) = \sum_{l=0}^{K} A[l] z^{-l}$. Step 3: Solve the $K \times K$ Vandermonde system $X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k u_k^m$ for the weights $c_k$.

nodes.name: Find annihilating filter coefficients
nodes.statement: Solve the Toeplitz/Yule-Walker linear system for $\{A[l]\}_{l=1}^{K}$ from $\sum_{l=0}^{K} A[l] X[m-l] = 0$ with $A[0]=1$, using at least $2K$ consecutive values $X[m]$. In practice, use SVD of the data matrix; for noisy data, take the right-singular-vector of the smallest singular value.

nodes.name: Root finding of $A(z)$
nodes.statement: Compute the $K$ roots of $A(z) = \sum_{l=0}^{K} A[l] z^{-l}$. These roots are the locations $u_k$.

nodes.name: Solve Vandermonde for weights
nodes.statement: Pick $K$ equations from $X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c_k u_k^m$ and solve the resulting $K \times K$ Vandermonde system for the weights $c_k$. The system is non-singular when $u_i \neq u_j$ for $i \neq j$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (Periodic Diracs sampling)
nodes.statement: Strategy: from the $N$ samples obtain $2M+1$ central Fourier series coefficients of $x(t)$, then apply the annihilating filter method to recover the locations and weights of the $K$ Diracs.

nodes.name: Recover Fourier series coefficients $X[m]$ from samples
nodes.statement: From $y_n = \langle h(t-nT), x(t)\rangle$ and $x(t) = \sum_m X[m] e^{j 2\pi m t/\tau}$, expand and obtain $Y[m'] = X[m'] H(m'/\tau)$ on the central band, which is invertible (DTFT of $H$) when $T$ is appropriately chosen.

nodes.name: Solve Yule-Walker for annihilating filter
nodes.statement: Given $\{X[m]\}_{m = -K}^{K-1}$, solve the Toeplitz system (24) for the $K$ filter coefficients $A[1], \ldots, A[K]$ of the annihilating filter (uniqueness from Proposition 3 in Appendix A).

nodes.name: Factor $A(z)$ to find Dirac locations
nodes.statement: Factor $A(z) = \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} (1 - u_k z^{-1})$; the roots $u_k = e^{-j 2\pi t_k/\tau}$ give the locations $t_k$.

nodes.name: Solve Vandermonde for Dirac weights
nodes.statement: Plug the recovered $u_k$ into $K$ Fourier-coefficient equations and solve the Vandermonde system (27) for the weights $c_k$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2 (Periodic Splines)
nodes.statement: Reduce to Theorem 1 by differentiating $R+1$ times: the result is a stream of $K$ weighted Diracs, recoverable by Theorem 1; the missing low-frequency Fourier coefficients of $x$ are then obtained by integration via (30).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3 (Differentiated Diracs)
nodes.statement: Use the annihilating filter for polynomial-weighted exponentials (Proposition 4): the annihilating filter has $K$ poles each of multiplicity $R_k$. Recover locations by root finding and weights by a generalized Vandermonde system.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4 (Piecewise Polynomials)
nodes.statement: Differentiate $(R+1)$ times to obtain a stream of differentiated Diracs and apply Theorem 3; recover the missing low-frequency coefficients via (30).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5 (Finite Diracs, Sinc Kernel)
nodes.statement: Multiply the Lagrange polynomial $\Lambda(t) = \prod_{l=0}^{N-1}(t-l)/(N-1)!$ by both sides of the sample equation and apply $K$ finite differences; the LHS vanishes (finite-difference operator acts as annihilating filter), giving $S \mathbf{B} = 0$. Solve for $B[i]$, find roots, then solve $H\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{u}$ for the weights.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6 (Finite Diracs, Gaussian Kernel)
nodes.statement: Substitution $u_k = e^{t_k T/\sigma^2}$, $a_k = c_k e^{-t_k^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ reduces the Gaussian-sampled equation to a sum of real exponentials, to which the annihilating filter method applies; the Toeplitz system in (68) admits a unique solution under the rank hypothesis.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1 (Box-Spline Bilevel)
nodes.statement: Sufficiency: with at most one transition per interval, the sample value $y_n = (n+1)T - t_k$ uniquely yields $t_k$. Necessity: two transitions $t_k, t_{k+1}$ in the same interval give $y_n = t_{k+1} - t_k$ and cannot be disentangled.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2 (Hat-Spline Bilevel)
nodes.statement: Sufficiency: enumerate all configurations of (number of transitions in $[nT,(n+1)T)$, number in $[(n+1)T,(n+2)T)$) summing to at most 2; for each, a quadratic system in the unknown transition locations admits a unique solution. Necessity: an explicit counterexample with three transitions in $[0,1]$ produces a quadratic system with infinitely many solutions.

nodes.name: Sufficiency: case enumeration
nodes.statement: List the configurations $(n_1, n_2)$ with $n_1 + n_2 \leq 2$ giving the number of transitions in $[nT,(n+1)T)$ and $[(n+1)T,(n+2)T)$: $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0)$. Each yields a quadratic system in the transition variables admitting a solution.

nodes.name: Uniqueness from sample-value test
nodes.statement: Use the values of $y_n, y_{n+1}$ to discriminate between configurations, e.g., $y_n = 0 \land y_{n+1} \neq 0$ implies $(0,1)$ or $(0,2)$, separated by the magnitude of $y_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Necessity by counterexample
nodes.statement: Three transitions in $[0,1]$ produce a degenerate quadratic system with infinitely many bilevel signals matching the same hat-spline samples; thus the at-most-two-transitions-per-$2T$ condition is necessary.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3 (Annihilating filter for sum of exponentials)
nodes.statement: Direct computation: $(A * X)[m] = \sum_l A[l] \sum_k c_k u_k^{m-l} = \sum_k c_k u_k^m \sum_l A[l] u_k^{-l} = \sum_k c_k u_k^m A(u_k) = 0$ since $A(u_k) = 0$ by construction.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4 (Multiple-root annihilator)
nodes.statement: Differentiate the identity $(1 - u_0 z^{-1})$ acting on $u_0^m$ to show that $(1 - u_0 z^{-1})^{r+1}$ kills $m^r u_0^m$ for any polynomial of degree $\leq r$; combine across distinct $u_k$ by convolution.

nodes.name: Whittaker-Shannon Sampling Theorem
nodes.statement: If $x(t)$ is bandlimited with $X(\omega) = 0$ for $|\omega| > \omega_0$, then the samples $y_n = x(nT)$ with $T = \pi/\omega_0$ are sufficient to reconstruct $x(t)$ via $x(t) = \sum_n y_n \operatorname{sinc}(t/T - n)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A bandlimited signal is recoverable from uniform samples taken above the Nyquist rate.

nodes.name: Periodic Stream of $K=8$ Diracs (Fig. 2)
nodes.statement: Periodic stream of $K=8$ weighted Diracs with period $\tau = 1024$ sampled with sinc kernel of bandwidth $B = 17/1024$ ($N = 17$ samples), illustrating Theorem 1; reconstruction is to machine precision. Annihilating filter shown in Fig. 3 with roots at the Dirac locations.

nodes.name: Periodic Nonuniform Linear Spline with $K=4$ Knots (Fig. 4)
nodes.statement: Periodic nonuniform linear spline with $K=4$ knots, period $\tau = 1024$, sampled with sinc kernel; reconstruction to machine precision.

nodes.name: Periodic Piecewise Linear Spline with $K=4$ Transitions (Fig. 5)
nodes.statement: Periodic piecewise linear spline with $K=4$ knots and period $\tau = 1024$, sampled with sinc kernel ($T = 32$); reconstruction within machine precision.

nodes.name: Bilevel Signal with Hat Sampling Kernel (Fig. 6)
nodes.statement: Bilevel signal with up to two transitions in any interval $[n, n+1]$ sampled with the hat sampling kernel $\beta^1(t/T)$ ($T=1$), illustrating Proposition 2.

nodes.name: Berlekamp-Massey alternative for factorization
nodes.statement: The factorization of $A(z)$ (Step 3 in the proof of Theorem 1) can be replaced by the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm from coding theory; in our setting, this amounts to a spectral extrapolation procedure (cf. Corollary 1).

nodes.name: Numerical stability of recursion
nodes.statement: $A(z)$ has zeros on the unit circle, so the recursion (28) is convolution with a marginally stable filter; in finite-precision arithmetic Corollary 1 is mostly of theoretical interest.

nodes.name: Oversampling and SVD for noisy data
nodes.statement: Conditioning of the matrices $S$ and $H$ degrades when the critical sample count is used; in practice, oversample and solve via SVD. The same approach handles noise: the annihilating-filter coefficients are then taken as the right-singular-vector of the smallest singular value.

nodes.name: Connection to spectral analysis and coding
nodes.statement: The annihilating filter is the error locator polynomial in error-correction coding and the high-resolution spectral estimator in spectral analysis (Stoica-Moses). The paper unifies these tools as a sampling primitive.

nodes.name: Multidimensional and broader-class FRI sampling
nodes.statement: Open: which other classes of signals with finite rate of innovation can be sampled and perfectly reconstructed? What tools beyond the annihilating filter can identify innovation? Are there computationally feasible multidimensional analogs of these results?
